Ohio Tree Species Guide — A Field Guide to NE Ohio's Yard Canopy

Twelve tree species cover most of the mature canopy you'll find in a Cuyahoga or Geauga County yard. This is the field-reference version — how to identify each species, the care it needs, the diseases it's prone to, and where to read the deeper care guide for each.

Learn to read a leaf, a strip of bark, and a branching pattern, and you can name almost any tree in a NE Ohio yard. For ten of the species below, Roubic keeps a dedicated care page — click through for the deeper guide.

Native, Naturalized, or Invasive?

Before identifying individual species, it helps to know which trees belong in a NE Ohio landscape and which are quietly working against it. The table below sorts the common yard trees into native, cultivated, and invasive.

SpeciesStatus in OhioNote
Oak (red, white, pin, bur)NativeFoundation canopy of NE Ohio. Plant whenever space allows.
Sugar mapleNativeOhio state tree. Slow but long-lived. Best fall color in the region.
Red mapleNativeFaster than sugar maple. Tolerates wet soils.
American beechNativeLong-lived, smooth gray bark, golden fall color. Sensitive to construction damage.
White ashNative (declining)Emerald ash borer has killed an estimated 90%+ since 2008. Replant other species.
Eastern white pineNativeFast evergreen. Tolerates clay soil. Good privacy screening.
Eastern red cedarNativeTough; tolerates poor soil. Watch for cedar-apple rust near apple trees.
Black cherry / ornamental cherryNative (black) / cultivated (ornamental)Watch for black knot disease.
American elm / Liberty / Princeton elmNative (American — declining) / resistant cultivarsDED-resistant cultivars now available.
Birch (river, paper)NativeWatch for bronze birch borer in stressed trees.
Tulip poplarNativeTall, fast, distinctive 4-lobed leaves. Drops branches in storms.
Willow (weeping, black)Native (black) / cultivated (weeping)Aggressive roots — keep distance from foundations.
Apple, pear, peach (fruit trees)CultivatedRoubic fruit-tree pruning service handles seasonal care.
Norway mapleInvasiveOutcompetes natives. Considered invasive in Ohio. Don't plant new ones.
Tree-of-heaven (Ailanthus)InvasiveAggressive spreader. Host for spotted lanternfly. Remove when found.
Callery pear ('Bradford' pear)InvasiveBanned for sale in Ohio as of 2023. Brittle structure; storm-failure-prone.

The 12 Tree Species You'll Most Often See in NE Ohio Yards

Each entry below covers identification, care timing, and the disease to watch for. Where a linked care guide exists, click the species name to read the full spoke page.

Oak

Care guide: Oak Tree Care

Identification: Lobed leaves; acorns; deeply furrowed bark. Species include red oak (sharply pointed lobes), white oak (rounded lobes, lighter bark), pin oak (small leaves, persistent dead lower branches), and bur oak (large leaves, distinctive corky bark).

Care: Oaks are slow-growing but extremely long-lived (200–300+ years for white oak). Dormant pruning only (late winter, never April–July). Tolerant of drought once established.

Disease watch: Oak wilt is the priority concern in NE Ohio. Outside-in browning leaves in summer plus rapid leaf drop means call an arborist immediately.

Sugar Maple

Care guide: Maple Tree Maintenance

Identification: Five-lobed leaves with smooth (un-toothed) edges; gray furrowed bark on mature trees; brilliant orange-to-red fall color. Don't confuse with Norway maple (toothed leaf edges, milky sap from a broken leaf petiole).

Care: Slow-growing, long-lived. Late-winter pruning preferred to minimize sap flow. Tolerant of partial shade.

Disease watch: Verticillium wilt and tar spot. Tar spot is cosmetic (black spots on leaves); verticillium can be terminal.

Red Maple

Care guide: Maple Tree Maintenance

Identification: Three-lobed (sometimes five) leaves; reddish twigs; red flowers in early spring; tolerates wet soils better than sugar maple.

Care: Fast-growing. Light pruning year-round acceptable; major pruning late winter.

Disease watch: Verticillium wilt; iron chlorosis on alkaline soils.

American Beech

Identification: Smooth gray bark (often graffiti-tempting); ovate leaves with prominent parallel veins; small triangular nuts in spiny husks; golden fall color. Distinctive.

Care: Long-lived but sensitive to soil disturbance and construction damage. Establish a critical root zone (1.5x dripline radius) and protect it during any nearby construction.

Disease watch: Beech bark disease and beech leaf disease (a newer concern). Watch for striations or blistering on bark and dark interveinal banding on leaves.

White Ash (Fraxinus americana)

Care guide: Ash Tree Disease Management

Identification: Compound leaves with 5–9 leaflets; opposite branching pattern (rare among large trees — only ash, maple, dogwood, horsechestnut); diamond-pattern furrowed bark.

Care: Population devastated by emerald ash borer. Smaller surviving trees may benefit from an emamectin benzoate trunk injection — call an arborist for evaluation.

Disease watch: Emerald ash borer (EAB) — D-shaped exit holes, bark splits, woodpecker damage. Plan removal once exit holes appear.

Eastern White Pine

Care guide: Pine Tree Trimming

Identification: Long flexible needles in clusters of five (mnemonic: 'W-H-I-T-E' = 5 letters); long narrow cones; tall pyramidal form when young.

Care: Fast-growing evergreen. Prune best in late winter or early spring; avoid summer pruning. Tolerates clay soils.

Disease watch: White pine blister rust; Diplodia tip blight; bark beetles in stressed trees.

Eastern Red Cedar (Juniperus virginiana)

Care guide: Cedar Tree Health & Maintenance

Identification: Scale-like overlapping leaves (not needles); blue-gray berries on female trees; reddish stringy bark; conical to columnar form.

Care: Tough; tolerates poor and dry soils. Pruning year-round acceptable; prefer late winter.

Disease watch: Cedar-apple rust — alternates between red cedar and apple/crabapple. Don't plant near orchards.

Cherry (black cherry + ornamental varieties)

Care guide: Cherry Tree Pruning

Identification: Black cherry has dark scaly bark, drooping clusters of small white flowers, and red-to-black drupes. Ornamental cherries have showy spring flowers (pink or white), often on grafted forms.

Care: Prune best in late winter or just after flowering. Watch for storm damage on weakly-attached scaffold branches.

Disease watch: Black knot — black gnarled growths on branches. Prune affected wood promptly. Brown rot affects fruiting cherries.

American Elm (and resistant cultivars)

Care guide: Elm Tree Preservation

Identification: Asymmetric leaf base (one side longer than the other); double-toothed leaf margins; vase-shaped overall form when mature; bark with gray and reddish layers.

Care: Original American elms are largely gone from NE Ohio due to Dutch elm disease (DED). Resistant cultivars — Liberty elm, Princeton elm, Valley Forge — are now standard for new plantings.

Disease watch: Dutch elm disease — flagging branches with wilted yellow leaves. Single-branch flagging caught early may respond to systemic fungicide; widespread flagging means removal.

Birch (river, paper)

Care guide: Birch Tree Care

Identification: Distinctive papery peeling bark — white in paper birch (Betula papyrifera), salmon-cinnamon in river birch (Betula nigra). Small ovate leaves with serrated edges.

Care: Avoid spring pruning — birch bleeds heavily during sap flow. Late summer or dormant pruning preferred.

Disease watch: Bronze birch borer — the primary concern. Stressed trees are most vulnerable; keep birches mulched and watered during drought.

Tulip Poplar (Liriodendron tulipifera)

Identification: Distinctive 4-lobed leaves (a tulip silhouette); orange-and-yellow tulip-shaped flowers in early summer; tall straight trunk; fast-growing.

Care: Fast-growing, can reach 80–100+ feet. Drops dead branches in storms — schedule deadwood removal regularly.

Disease watch: Verticillium wilt and yellow-poplar weevil. Generally hardy.

Willow / Weeping Willow

Care guide: Willow Tree Care

Identification: Long narrow leaves with finely-toothed edges; characteristic drooping branches in weeping varieties; deeply ridged bark on mature trees.

Care: Aggressive root system — plant 50+ feet from foundations, septic, and drains. Late-winter pruning preferred. Tolerates wet soils.

Disease watch: Crown gall, willow scab, and fungal cankers in stressed trees.

Fruit Trees (apple, pear, peach, plum)

Care guide: Fruit Tree Pruning & Maintenance

Identification: Varies by species. Apple: ovate-toothed leaves, white-pink flowers, fruit. Pear: glossy ovate leaves, white flowers. Peach: long lance-shaped leaves, pink flowers. Plum: similar to cherry but with plum fruit.

Care: Annual pruning is essential for fruit yield and tree health. Late-winter dormant pruning is the standard window. Roubic offers fruit-tree-specific maintenance contracts.

Disease watch: Apple scab; fire blight (pears, apples); brown rot (peaches, plums); cedar-apple rust (apples).

Disease Susceptibility — Quick Reference

The single fastest way to protect a tree is to know its one likeliest problem. This table pairs each species group with its top disease concern.

SpeciesTop disease concernNote
Oak (all species)Oak wiltHighest priority NE Ohio disease concern
AshEmerald ash borer (EAB)90%+ of ash population killed since 2008
Elm (American)Dutch elm diseaseResistant cultivars (Liberty, Princeton) recommended for new plantings
Maple (all species)Verticillium wilt, tar spotTar spot cosmetic; verticillium terminal
BeechBeech bark disease, beech leaf diseaseBeech leaf disease is a newer concern; growing across Ohio
PineWhite pine blister rust, DiplodiaStress-related; keep watered during drought
BirchBronze birch borerStressed birch most vulnerable
Cherry / fruit treesBlack knot, fire blight, brown rotAnnual pruning of affected wood essential
Cedar (red)Cedar-apple rustDon't plant near apple/crabapple
WillowCrown gall, fungal cankerStress-related; aggressive roots are the bigger concern
Tulip poplarVerticillium wilt, yellow-poplar weevilGenerally hardy

What to Plant in NE Ohio Today

If you're replacing trees lost to EAB or storm damage, or planting new canopy on a redesigned property, the species mix to favor in 2026 is different than it was 20 years ago. Below are the species worth planting now, plus what to avoid.

Recommended for new plantings

Recommended speciesWhy
Oak — white oak, bur oakLong-lived foundation canopy. Plant whenever space allows.
Sugar mapleSlow but unmatched fall color and longevity.
American beechDistinctive smooth bark, golden fall, long-lived.
Resistant elm cultivars — Liberty, Princeton, Valley ForgeBring back the elm canopy without DED risk.
Tulip poplarFast canopy filler; tall straight form.
Eastern white pinePrivacy screening; clay-tolerant.
River birchHardier than paper birch; wet-soil tolerant.

Avoid planting

Three species to avoid: Norway maple (invasive in Ohio, outcompetes natives), tree-of-heaven / Ailanthus (aggressive invasive, hosts spotted lanternfly), and Callery / Bradford pear (banned for sale in Ohio as of 2023, brittle structure that fails in storms). Original American elms (non-resistant cultivars) are also a poor choice given Dutch elm disease pressure — use Liberty or Princeton instead.

The single most important thing a NE Ohio homeowner can do for their trees is simple: never prune an oak between April and July. One summer cut can introduce oak wilt and kill a 150-year-old tree in two seasons. Timing beats technique. {{global.owner_name}} · Owner, Roubic Tree & Landscape

Common Species Questions

Ohio Tree Species FAQ

What's the most common tree in NE Ohio yards?
Maple — both red maple and sugar maple — is the most common large tree in established NE Ohio yards, followed by oak (mixed species), American beech, ash (declining due to EAB), and white pine. Mature suburban canopy in the inner-ring villages of Greater Cleveland is dominated by oaks and maples that were planted 60–100+ years ago.
How can I tell what kind of tree I have?
Three quick checks: leaf shape (lobed, simple, compound, needle-like), bark pattern (smooth, furrowed, peeling, scaly), and branching habit (opposite vs alternate). Opposite branching is rare and points to maple, ash, dogwood, or horsechestnut; everything else is alternate. If you're stuck, photograph the leaf, bark, and overall form and call {{global.phone}} — we can usually ID a tree from a phone photo.
Is my ash tree definitely going to die from EAB?
Most untreated mature ash in NE Ohio that haven't already died eventually will. The regional emerald ash borer outbreak began in 2008 and has now killed an estimated 90%+ of ash trees in Cuyahoga and Geauga counties. Smaller, otherwise-healthy ash can sometimes be preserved with annual emamectin benzoate trunk injections, but treatment must begin before significant damage and is most cost-effective on smaller trees. Plan removal for any ash showing D-shaped exit holes and crown dieback.
What tree should I plant to replace a dead ash?
It depends on the spot. For a similar-sized canopy tree, sugar maple, white oak, bur oak, or American beech are excellent long-term choices. For faster establishment, tulip poplar or red maple. Avoid replanting another ash — the EAB pressure isn't going away. The recommended-plantings table above lists the best 2026 choices.
Why does Roubic refuse to prune oak trees in summer?
Oak wilt is a fungal disease vectored by sap-feeding nitidulid beetles, and the high-risk window in Ohio runs roughly April 1 through July 31. Pruning during that window creates fresh wounds the beetles are attracted to, and a single infected cut can introduce oak wilt that kills the tree within two seasons and spreads to adjacent oaks through root grafts. We won't prune your oak in May or June regardless of urgency.
